title: Narrative character networks are associated with storytelling success
authors: Xuanjun Gong, Allison Eden, Frederic R Hopp, Anna W Wolfe, Matthew Grizzard
abstract: Narratives are central to human communication and entertainment, yet why some stories captivate audiences better than others remains poorly understood. Building on theories emphasizing character interdependence, this study introduces a network-based framework for examining storytelling success. We conceptualize narratives as networks composed of characters and their interactions and apply large-scale computational analysis to over 10,000 novels and 1,000 film screenplays. Structural features of these networks are related to storytelling success: lower clustering is associated with greater novel popularity and higher film ratings, whereas higher modularity is associated only with novel popularity and shorter path lengths only with film ratings. These findings demonstrate that storytelling success is related to how characters are structurally connected and organized. By formalizing story architecture as a measurable network, we provide a scalable framework for advancing media entertainment theory, linking cognitive models of graph learning with the structural organization of stories at scale.

title: Does transparency matter when interacting with social bots? An experiment on user engagement behaviors in Chinese social media
authors: Hao Xu, Shaobo Liang, Qingxuan Cheng
abstract: Purpose While transparency is widely promoted as a principle of responsible AI design, its behavioral consequences remain contested, particularly in Chinese social media contexts. This study examines whether different levels of social bot transparency reduce or facilitate user engagement, and whether these effects depend on users' prior knowledge of social bots. Design/methodology/approach An online experiment was conducted in a simulated Weibo environment. A total of 731 participants were randomly assigned to one of three transparency conditions: low, medium, or high transparency. User engagement behaviors were measured through participants' behavioral choices, including reading, liking/sharing, replying, and combined engagement actions. Multinomial logistic regression and subgroup analyses were used to examine the effects of transparency and the moderating role of prior knowledge. Findings Social bot transparency significantly reduces active user engagement. Compared with high transparency, low transparency increases the likelihood of liking/sharing, replying, and combined reply-based engagement rather than merely reading. Medium transparency produces engagement patterns similar to high transparency, suggesting that even ambiguous bot identity cues may activate non-human attribution and suppress active engagement. Prior knowledge moderates this relationship: users with limited prior knowledge are more sensitive to transparency cues, whereas those with higher prior knowledge show more stable engagement across transparency conditions. Originality/value This study extends social bot transparency research beyond binary disclosure by identifying a categorical identity-attribution mechanism. It also clarifies prior knowledge as a boundary condition of algorithm aversion in human-AI interaction.

title: Beyond Human–AI interaction: exploring the influence of AI anthropomorphism on work engagement
authors: Bin Ling, Yuting Xia, Yujie Cai
abstract: Purpose This study examines how anthropomorphic cues that make AI agency socially salient influence employee work engagement in mandatory, performance-oriented human–AI collaboration. It distinguishes AI agency from AI anthropomorphism, tests affective and evaluative motivational mechanisms and identifies perceived AI threat as a boundary condition grounded in the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model. Design/methodology/approach Across two pilot studies and two main experiments (total N = 501), we used immersive workplace role-playing scenarios to test a dual-pathway model. Integrating social response theory with the JD-R model, this research tests a dual-pathway model in which anthropomorphic design influences work engagement through emotional bonding and acquisitive impression management motive (IMM), whereas perceived artificial intelligence threat operates as a hindrance demand that weakens these resource pathways. Findings Anthropomorphic AI enhanced work engagement through two motivational routes: an affective route via emotional bonding and an evaluative route via IMM. However, perceived AI threat significantly attenuated these benefits. When threat was high, the positive effects of anthropomorphism on emotional bonding, IMM and work engagement became non-significant, suggesting that replacement-related threat drains the psychological capacity needed for anthropomorphic cues to function as job resources. Originality/value This research contributes to workplace AI and information systems (IS) scholarship by clarifying how anthropomorphic cues make AI agency socially salient without equating anthropomorphism with agency. It extends prior work on anthropomorphic AI and engagement by identifying an evaluative pathway – performing for AI – alongside the affective pathway of bonding with AI. It also offers a contingency-based explanation for the anthropomorphism paradox by showing that the benefits of humanlike design depend on the surrounding AI-threat climate.

title: When it’s your own child: effects of media narratives on U.S. parents’ support for their LGBTQ+ teen
authors: Marie-Louise Mares, Y Anthony Chen
abstract: Parents’ responses to their LGBTQ+ child are varied, often intense, and have important consequences for the child. To examine how media depictions may shape responses, a pre-registered online experiment of 494 parents tested effects of viewing two TV narratives, depicting either control (non-LGBTQ+) family interactions, parental rejection, gradual growth toward acceptance, or unalloyed acceptance, of a lesbian or transgender teen, on parents’ support and behavioral intentions regarding their own LGBTQ+ teen. Guided by theories of vicarious contact and inspiring media, we assessed mediation via identification with characters, and via feelings of inspiration and manipulation, testing baseline support as a moderator. Effects of condition were indirect-only, and contingent on baseline support. Among highly supportive parents, growth and acceptance narratives (vs. control) increased feelings of inspiration, which predicted positive behavioral intentions. Among less supportive parents, rejection and (unexpectedly) growth narratives reduced identification with depicted LGBTQ+ teens, indirectly decreasing support and behavioral intentions.

title: Enhancing Online Deliberation Through AI-Driven Counter-Attitudinal Interventions: Direct and Indirect Effects on Users’ Perceptions and Behavior
authors: Jana Leonie Peters, Marc Ziegele, Carina Weinmann
abstract: This study tests whether an AI-based counter-attitudinal comment recommender (AI-CAR) enhances participants’ subjective deliberative experiences and reduces incivility by restructuring the visibility of dissenting viewpoints. We analyzed three-wave data from 827 participants in a 10-day simulated digital citizens’ council in Germany. Participants discussed one of two political issues asynchronously and were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: counter-attitudinal AI recommendations, randomly selected recommendations, or no recommendations. Assignment to AI-CAR increased perceived equality of viewpoints. Higher perceived equality at wave 2 was associated with greater internal deliberation and discussion satisfaction at wave 3, controlling for their wave-2 levels. The corresponding model-based indirect effects were statistically significant, whereas comparable indirect effects were not statistically significant for randomly selected recommendations. AI-CAR did not reduce incivility in participants’ contributions. Overall, the findings highlight the potential of AI-driven structural curation to support subjective deliberative experiences, while effects on incivility remain limited.
journal_full: Journal of Language and Social Psychology

title: Extending the Deservingness Framework to Communication Sciences
authors: David De Coninck, Lise-Lore Steeman
abstract: While communication research has documented how media frame social groups as victims or threats, little is known about the evaluative criteria through which mediated discourse constructs minority representations. This study introduces deservingness as a framework for analyzing such evaluative logics, drawing on the Control, Attitude, Reciprocity, Identity, Need (CARIN) criteria. We illustrate this through an analysis of 7,561 Belgian newspaper articles across three migration contexts (2015, 2021, 2022), combining automated dictionary-based content analysis with a theory-driven qualitative content analysis of 284 articles. Results reveal a stable but context-sensitive deservingness communication. We position deservingness as a transferable tool for research on moral evaluation and conditional solidarity.

title: Promoting Support for Anti-Racism Movements and Intentions to Intervene: Effects of Common-Identity Narratives and the Moderating Role of Prior Prejudice
authors: Yan Huang, Lan Ni, Zexin Ma, Natasha Saad
abstract: Two experiments examined whether emphasizing a common ingroup identity with racially different characters, operationalized as university affiliation with an African American character (Study 1) and parent identity with an Asian American character (Study 2), enhanced the impact of victim narratives. Findings indicate that emphasizing a common ingroup identity increased perceived similarity and identification with the character and reduced perceived social distance, which then fostered greater support toward anti-racism movements and stronger intentions to intervene. Common-identity narratives were particularly effective among participants with higher prior prejudice, and the moderation effect was mediated by reduced social distance.

title: Perceived Sources Matter: Implications of Misinformation on Media Trust and News Avoidance Under Different Levels of Press Freedom
authors: Yuteng Zheng, Michael Chan, Francis L. F. Lee
abstract: Extant research on the impact of misinformation on media trust and news avoidance behavior has produced competing arguments and findings. The present study argues that the relationships among misinformation, media trust, and news avoidance can be better specified by considering whether people perceive misinformation as coming primarily from established institutions or non-institutional sources. Given the close linkage between the mainstream news media and established social and political institutions, people are likely to exhibit lower levels of news trust and higher levels of news avoidance if they perceive misinformation as coming from institutional sources. In contrast, when people perceive misinformation as coming from non-institutional sources, they may rely on the news media as authoritative fact-checkers and hence trust the news more and avoid it less. Societal-level press freedom is likely to moderate such relationships. The arguments and hypotheses are tested by an analysis of Digital News Report 2025 data.

title: TikTok News: How The Washington Post ’s Use of Platform Logics Affects Perceptions of Journalists and News Learning
authors: Audrey Halversen, Brian E. Weeks
abstract: In a period of high competition, many contemporary journalists attract audience attention by adopting the stylistic conventions (“logics”) of platforms like TikTok to deliver news online. However, the effects of this content on audience trust and learning remain unclear. Using two online experiments, we examine whether audiences perceive journalists as credible and learn from news videos employing TikTok logics, compared to traditional print articles. Results indicate that journalists using TikTok logics may effectively capture attention but are viewed as less trustworthy, credible, professional, and knowledgeable, though more likable, than print journalists. Learning outcomes are similar across formats.

title: Transnationalization of Anti-Gender Politics on Social Media: Hashtag Practices and Cross-Border Visibility
authors: Dominika Tronina
abstract: Gender politics have become central arenas of contemporary political struggle, with anti-gender movements mobilizing across borders to contest women’s and LGBTQI+ rights. While research has shown that anti-gender actors articulate strikingly similar positions across national contexts, it remains insufficiently understood how such similarity translates into shared transnational action. This study examines how anti-gender movements collectively generate transnational visibility on social media by analyzing ten years of Twitter (now X) communication from 148 anti-gender social movement organizations in Croatia, Germany, France, Italy, and Poland (<em>N</em> = 126,711 tweets). Drawing on concepts of networked framing and discourse coalitions, this study employs a mixed-methods analysis of hashtag co-usage on Twitter, combining quantitative measures of transnational hashtag connectivity with qualitative thematic content analysis. The findings reveal that anti-gender movements co-create visibility for opposition to gender equality through a threefold pattern, including a continuous dissemination of ideological narratives, an episodic activation of campaigns, and a strategic extension of anti-gender frames into broader public debates. These practices enable actors to jointly enhance the visibility and persistence of anti-gender claims across multiple publics while simultaneously adapting frames to divergent political contexts. By linking cross-border hashtag practices to the co-production of visibility, this study contributes to research on gendered public spheres by demonstrating how similarity among anti-gender actors becomes transnationally consequential through the joint production of visibility in networked communication environments.

title: Practicing love with algorithms: How online communities narrate and make sense of human–AI intimacy
authors: Fanjue Liu, Haiyan Hao, Kun Xu
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes embedded in everyday life, emotionally intimate interactions with AI companions are becoming increasingly visible. Yet prior research has focused mainly on individual experiences, leaving limited understanding of how human–AI intimacy is collectively interpreted and negotiated in online communities. This study examines community discourse on RedNote, a major Chinese social and lifestyle platform, using 13,059 comments from 58 relevant posts. Combining BERTopic modeling with a human–large language model (LLM) hybrid emotion classification procedure, the analysis identifies three thematic clusters: intimacy as co-construction, intimacy as infrastructure, and intimacy as boundary negotiation. Co-construction centers on persona design, roleplay, and narrative world-building and is marked mainly by joy and curiosity. Infrastructure-related discourse is associated with frustration and sadness, while boundary negotiation reflects ambivalence toward intimacy with AI.

title: Understanding how exposure to science content on social media shapes normative expectations of scientists’ communication: A social media affordances perspective
authors: Annie Li Zhang
abstract: As social media continue to shape where science is communicated and how it is consumed, this study adopts an affordances approach to advance our understanding of how audiences observe and make sense of online scientific content and evaluate science and scientists more broadly. By analyzing a two-wave survey ( N = 878) conducted in February and March 2025, this study reveals that online science content exposure is associated with increased normative expectations across a range of scientists’ communication behaviors, including political advocacy, warmth- and competence-oriented strategies, and public engagement. In addition, stronger expectations of competency-oriented communication and political advocacy were associated with greater trust in and vulnerability toward scientists. Political ideology was found to moderate the relationship between science observation and certain normative expectations. Findings underscore the role of social media in influencing science communication norms and (re)shaping what it means to be a trustworthy scientist in an increasingly visible and networked media environment.

title: Conflict With Context: The Impact of Explanations of Scientific Uncertainty and Informant Differences on Responses to Conflicting Health Advice
authors: Yanmengqian Zhou, Youzhen Su
abstract: This experiment examined whether conflict explanations (informant-based, uncertainty-based, vs. none) and conflict framing (alternative vs. opposing) mitigate negative responses to conflicting health advice. Both explanations reduced perceived conflict, with informant-based explanations effective only among individuals with lower perceived knowledge. No significant effect of conflict framing was observed. Perceived conflict was subsequently associated with greater confusion, uncertainty, anger, and anxiety. Uncertainty, in turn, was more strongly associated with topic-specific attitude ambivalence, whereas anger was more strongly associated with generalized health confusion and backlash. Mediation analysis further supported several indirect effects of conflict explanations on downstream outcomes through these pathways.

title: Do Experts Agree About Misinformation? Evidence From Three Annual Surveys
authors: Sacha Altay, Sebastián Valenzuela, Philip N. Howard
abstract: How much do experts on the information environment agree about the scale, spread, and effects of misinformation? We drew on three annual waves of the International Panel on the Information Environment expert survey to examine agreement with seven popular claims about misinformation (2023: N = 262; 2024: N = 413; 2025: N = 442; spanning 76 countries). Agreement varied widely across statements and was stable across waves. About 60% of experts agreed that falsehoods spread faster than the truth and that misinformation is widespread. About half agreed that misinformation has a substantial influence on behavior and that people readily believe what they see online; about 40% agreed that more people have become misinformed over time; and only 25% agreed that misinformation is primarily a social media problem. The surveys also revealed a persistent divide between experts who saw misinformation as widespread and consequential and those more skeptical, with sharpest disagreement on its behavioral impact and increase over time. In 2025, some experts distinguished between misperception prevalence and misinformation severity. Overall agreement varied by respondent background: agreement was higher among experts on developing countries than those on developed countries, higher among STEM researchers than social scientists, and lower among political scientists than communication scholars. Expert consensus on misinformation is partial, varies across claims and experts, and is shaped by geography and discipline.

title: Exploring the Predictors and Outcomes of Perceived Algorithm Responsiveness in Social Media Feeds: Combining Longitudinal and Computational Methods
authors: Samuel Hardman Taylor, David M. Markowitz
abstract: Perceptions of how algorithms curate content are integral to how people use social media and its effects. Building on the algorithm responsiveness process, we explore whether perceived algorithm responsiveness (PAR) was associated with the message cues of algorithmically curated content. We coupled longitudinal data from a 7-day, twice-daily diary survey with computational digital traces from Twitter (now X) to operationalize algorithmic message characteristics and to understand the antecedents and outcomes of PAR ( N = 10,337 tweets). Results suggested that message cues from algorithmic content in social feeds (i.e., closeness, popularity, valence, and format) were associated with perceived message personalization, but message personalization was the only message characteristic associated with PAR. PAR predicted feeling more connected to others on Twitter, along with message-level factors: closeness to the poster and message personalization. This work contributes to the algorithm responsiveness process, demonstrating that characteristics of algorithmically curated messages predict how individuals experience algorithms.

title: Losing the engaged without winning the disengaged: Personalism and the choice of political news
authors: Troels Bøggild, Helene Helboe Pedersen
abstract: When political news centers on the policy work or private lives of individual politicians rather than on parties, it can obscure the collective actors citizens must judge at elections. The usual defense is that such personalism attracts readers, especially those otherwise unlikely to choose political news. We test this claim in survey experiments in Denmark, the United Kingdom, and the United States ( N = 3039). Respondents chose between an entertainment article and a political article whose subheadline attributed a new bill to a party, an individual politician (individualized), or the politician’s personal story (privatized). Personalism recruited no readers. Effects are negative in all countries and pooled amount to a significant five percentage point loss. The losses were concentrated among politically engaged citizens, while the least engaged, the very readers personalism is meant to attract, were unmoved. Party-centered news thus entail no audience sacrifice as citizens prefer the format that keeps parties visible.

title: Generalizing Causal Effects with Noncompliance: Application to Deep Canvassing Experiments
authors: Zhongren Chen, Melody Huang
abstract: Standard approaches in generalizability often focus on generalizing the intent-to-treat effect. However, in practice, a more policy-relevant quantity is the generalized impact of an intervention across compliers. While instrumental variable methods are commonly used to estimate the complier average causal effect (CACE) within samples, standard approaches cannot be applied to a target population with a different distribution from the study sample. This article makes several key contributions. First, we introduce a new set of identifying assumptions in the form of a population-level exclusion restriction that allows for identification of the target CACE (T-CACE) in both randomized experiments and observational studies. This allows researchers to identify the T-CACE without relying on standard principal ignorability assumptions. Second, we propose a class of inverse-weighted estimators for the T-CACE and derive their asymptotic properties. We provide extensions for settings in which researchers have access to auxiliary compliance information across the target population. Finally, we introduce a sensitivity analysis for researchers to evaluate the robustness of the estimators in the presence of unmeasured confounding and extend existing tests to evaluate instrument validity in this context. We illustrate our proposed method through extensive simulations and a study evaluating the impact of deep canvassing on reducing exclusionary attitudes.

title: Beliefs About Public Opinion and the Perceived Legitimacy of Policy Decisions
authors: Nils D. Steiner, Claudia Landwehr
abstract: Democratic legitimacy is typically thought to depend on whether political decisions reflect public opinion, or majority preferences. Do citizens share this standard? And what if citizens are wrong about public opinion? We study how beliefs about public support for controversial policy proposals are associated with the perceived legitimacy of adopting them, and whether accurate polling information changes these judgments. In a representative survey experiment in Germany, respondents reported their own position on four such proposals, estimated public support, and rated the legitimacy of adopting each one. For a random subset of proposals, respondents received accurate polling information showing that the proposal lacked majority support. We find that perceived public support predicts legitimacy judgments even after accounting for respondents’ own policy preferences. Yet these perceptions are often inaccurate and shaped by respondents’ own views. Corrective polling information modestly lowers perceived legitimacy, especially among those who initially overestimated public support. The findings suggest that misperceptions of public opinion can distort, but accurate information can also partly correct, citizens’ assessments of democratic legitimacy.

title: Ideology at first sight: a comparative study of ideological stereotypes in four European countries
authors: Gaetano Scaduto, Fedra Negri, Silvia Decadri
abstract: In recent years, research on political stereotypes has expanded, showing that trait-based associations about members of political groups are both pervasive and consequential for intergroup relations and polarization. Yet it is unclear which traits are more often involved in stereotypes about ideological groups. Moreover, this literature is overwhelmingly focused on the USA and severely lacks comparative evidence. This paper addresses these gaps by examining how sociodemographic, personality, and lifestyle characteristics are associated with citizens’ perceptions of others’ political ideology in Czechia, France, Italy, and Sweden. Findings from a conjoint experiment indicate that both sociodemographic and lifestyle traits, particularly professions and means of transportation, can inform citizens’ ideological perceptions. Conversely, personality traits demonstrate relatively limited influence. Comparative analyses reveal both common patterns and noteworthy heterogeneity: Sweden emphasizes class-related traits, France and Italy prioritize religious and age factors, while Czechia exhibits markedly distinct patterns.
journal_full: International Journal of Public Opinion Research

title: Structural Bias in Stylized Items with Point-Valued Categories
authors: Ettore Scappini
abstract: Survey research frequently relies on stylized questions with discrete, ordered response categories to measure behaviors or attitudes. While these items simplify responses and facilitate standardization, they introduce a structural bias component (SBC) arising from the discrepancy between actual behavior and the assigned category values. This paper investigates SBC in the context of religious practice, using data from the European Values Study across multiple waves and countries. The analysis shows that the discrete nature of point-value items can generate distortions. A calibration model is proposed to estimate and adjust for this bias, assuming a uniform distribution of behaviors within each interval. Findings suggest that, while SBC can reach substantial levels in some domains—particularly where the accuracy of absolute values is crucial—in practice, however, its impact on theoretical interpretations or explanatory factors is typically limited. The study underscores the importance of carefully designing response categories and considering alternative scaling methods, such as stylized items with interval-valued categories, to reduce measurement error and enhance survey validity.
journal_full: Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology

title: Investigating the Utility of LLM-Based “Silicon Samples” in Political Science Conjoint Experiments
authors: Alice Malmberg
abstract: This research note is the first study to explore the viability of using LLM-generated respondents in forced-choice conjoint experiments. I generate naive “silicon samples” using three models, GPT 4o-Mini, Llama 3.2, and Magistral-small-2506, benchmarked to a large sample of live conjoint respondents, allowing for direct comparisons between human and silicon choices. The resulting analyses suggest that naively generated silicon samples are insufficient to simulate human decision-making in conjoint tasks; these results also suggest that there are systemic differences in the way demographic covariates shape LLM and human choices in experimental contexts. In total, this analysis makes two important contributions: it establishes a descriptive baseline understanding of LLM-generated respondent performance in conjoint experiments and suggests that naive silicon samples cannot accurately infer human choices using demographic traits in experimental decision making contexts. Finally, the implications of these results imply that LLMs consider covariates differently than live respondents do in micro-level decision making contexts.

title: Do Gender-of-Interviewer Effects Differ Across Immigrant Generations? Survey Evidence from Italy
authors: Christina Sarah Hauser
abstract: Interviewer gender has been shown to affect responses to survey questions on gender attitudes and norms, but does its influence vary across groups with different migration backgrounds? I study this question using the Between Origin and Destination (BOnD) survey, conducted in Lombardy, Italy, between 2024 and 2025. Consistent with gender-of-interviewer effects, a type of social desirability bias, female interviewers elicit more progressive responses on a summary index of gender norms and on an index of the acceptability of homosexuality, abortion, divorce, casual sex, and premarital sex. The effect is concentrated among natives and second-generation individuals; first-generation immigrants show little response to interviewer gender. One possible explanation is that social desirability pressure from a female interviewer operates through host-country social norms: Individuals more embedded in the Italian normative context are more responsive to cues from a female interviewer. These findings have implications for the design of surveys administered to mixed native-immigrant populations.

title: Agreement Helps, Disagreement Matters: Scaling Framing Function Annotation With Large Language Models
authors: Emily Robinson, Ranadheer Malla, Chico Q. Camargo
abstract: Framing research has long relied on human annotation, but many aspects of framing – especially framing functions such as defining problems, identifying causes, making moral evaluations, or proposing solutions are difficult to label consistently and at scale. We demonstrate that large language models can reliably identify these framing functions, achieving levels of agreement comparable to those of human annotators. We evaluate three state-of-the-art models (GPT-5, Claude 3.7, and DeepSeek) alongside three trained human coders on a new dataset of social media posts about electric-vehicles, a highly topical and contested issue that holds many interpretations. This setting provides a strong test of both agreement and meaningful disagreement in framing-function annotation. Across models and humans, we find not only substantial convergence but also patterns of valid disagreement – differences that reflect legitimate alternative interpretations rather than annotation error. Recognising and preserving these cases enhances construct validity and provides a more realistic portrayal of how framing functions operate in contested debates. Our results demonstrate that large language models can scale framing function analysis while capturing the variability inherent in human interpretation, enabling forms of communication research that were previously impractical with human-only coding.

title: Multiple Methods for Visualizing Human Language: A Tutorial for Social and Behavioral Scientists
authors: Veerle C. Eijsbroek, August H. Nilsson, Leon Ackermann, Zhuojun Gu, Clara Wiebel, Adithya V. Ganesan, Katarina Kjell, H. Andrew Schwartz, Oscar N. E. Kjell
abstract: Humans use language to communicate psychological experiences. Advancements in natural language processing have enabled researchers to quantitatively study and assess psychological states and behaviors through language. Insights from these language analyses are often best conveyed through visualizations. Data-driven visualizations of how language statistically relates to psychological dimensions can help interpret assessment scores, uncover meaningful patterns, and understand the intricate relationships between language use and mental states. Visualizations can be used to differentiate between related constructs (e.g., How does language related to depression versus anxiety differ?), understand the validity of assessment tools (e.g., Does the language related to high depression severity match with depression theory?), and explain language-based assessments (e.g., Which language is indicative of higher depression severity in a language-based assessment?). In this tutorial, we demonstrate how to transform language data into visual insights using the text and topics packages in R. We provide practical guidance on creating four types of visualizations based on different language-analysis techniques, examining how language-use patterns are statistically associated with psychological constructs. We visualize (a) individual words and phrases (n-grams), (b) topics (word clusters), (c) words in the word-embedding space, and (d) relevant language examples. The different visualizations offer complementary perspectives, visualizing linguistic elements from individual words to overarching topics and text examples. The underlying methods range from correlations between individual words to more advanced techniques, including topic modeling and large language models. By making these methods accessible, we aim to empower researchers to use language visualizations for meaningful, data-driven insights.
journal_full: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science

title: Large language models for computational social science
authors: Fengli Xu, Chenyang Shao, Lin Chen, Qingbin Zeng, Zhilong Chen, Nicholas Sukiennik, Jingyi Wang, Chen Gao, Huandong Wang, Jianxun Lian, Qingguo Meng, Xing Xie, Yong Li, James Evans
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming computational social science. This Review examines how LLMs now serve four distinct research roles: subjects that simulate human behaviour, assistants that automate analysis, collaborators that generate hypotheses and evaluators that audit and improve research quality. We analyse recent advances across sociology, political science, psychology, anthropology, economics and related fields, revealing how LLMs accelerate discovery while creating new methodological paradigms. This transformation arrives as society itself becomes saturated with artificial intelligence agents—making LLMs both our research tools and authentic research subjects. Yet fundamental challenges persist. LLMs struggle with causal inference and raise urgent ethical concerns about privacy and misinformation, and their ability to reproduce social complexity remains uneven and unproven. We identify critical research directions for harnessing LLMs’ potential while addressing their limitations. As artificial intelligence reshapes human society, understanding this transformation requires the very tools driving it—a recursive challenge that will define the future of social science.
